title: Śvetāmbara Āgamas (the Jain canon)
summary: The canonical scriptures of the Śvetāmbara Jains: the twelve-limbed 'basket of the gaṇin' (duvālasaṅga gaṇipiḍaga) of which eleven Aṅgas survive, together with the 'outside the limbs' (aṅgabāhya) texts. Mūrtipūjakas count forty-five texts (11 Aṅgas, 12 Upāṅgas, 10 Prakīrṇakas, 6 Chedasūtras, 4 Mūlasūtras, 2 Cūlikāsūtras); Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs accept thirty-two. The Digambaras hold that the original Aṅgas were lost and do not accept this collection.

attribution.tradition: The Aṅgas go back to the gaṇadharas' composition of Mahāvīra's teaching; the aṅgabāhya texts to later elders (sthaviras); recited at the councils of Pāṭaliputra, Mathurā and Valabhī and written down at Valabhī under Devarddhigaṇi (980 or 993 years after the nirvāṇa).
attribution.scholarly: Compiled from materials of very different ages (c. 4th c. BCE – 5th c. CE); the grouping into Upāṅgas, Chedas, Mūlas and Prakīrṇakas and the count of 45 are medieval (the Nandī classifies differently: aṅga-praviṣṭa / aṅga-bāhya, kālika / utkālika).

tradition.text: taught by Mahāvīra (d. 527 BCE by the traditional reckoning); written down at Valabhī 453 or 466 CE

scholarly.text: oldest layers c. 4th–3rd c. BCE; closed in the 5th c. CE

structure.description: 45 texts (Mūrtipūjaka) or 32 (Sthānakavāsī, Terāpanthī); see cpt:svetambara-canon-45 and cpt:sthanakavasi-canon-32

title: Ācārāṅga Sūtra
summary: The first Aṅga, on the conduct (ācāra) of the mendicant. Book I (Bambhacerāiṃ, 'the discipline of chastity'; nine lectures, the seventh, Mahāparijñā, lost) teaches non-harm to the six classes of living beings (earth, water, fire, plants, mobile beings, wind), detachment and vigilance, and ends with the Upadhānaśruta, the account of Mahāvīra's austerities. Book II (four cūlās) gives detailed rules on alms, lodging, walking, speech, clothing and bowls, and a life of Mahāvīra with the twenty-five bhāvanās of the five great vows.

attribution.tradition: The meaning (artha) was taught by Mahāvīra; the gaṇadhara Sudharman composed the sūtras and transmitted them to Jambū ('suyaṃ me āusaṃ…', 'I have heard, O long-lived one'); redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous compilation with layers of different ages, fixed in writing at Valabhī in the 5th c. CE.

tradition.text: spoken by Mahāvīra and composed by Sudharman

scholarly.text: Book I among the oldest Jain texts (often placed c. 4th–3rd c. BCE); Book II later

structure.description: 2 śrutaskandhas: I = 9 lectures (adhyayana), 44 lessons (uddeśaka), the 7th lecture lost; II = 4 cūlās in 16 lectures (the 5th cūlā became the Niśītha)

title: Sūtrakṛtāṅga
summary: The second Aṅga, largely polemical: it states and rejects the views of other teachers (materialists, the one-self doctrine, the soul-is-the-body doctrine, non-agency, fatalism, Buddhist momentariness), classifies all rival doctrines under four heads (kriyāvāda, akriyāvāda, ajñānavāda, vinayavāda), warns the monk against temptations, praises Mahāvīra, and in Book II gives the parable of the lotus, Ārdraka's debates with rival ascetics and the Nālandā dialogue with a follower of Pārśva.

attribution.tradition: The meaning (artha) was taught by Mahāvīra; the gaṇadhara Sudharman composed the sūtras and transmitted them to Jambū ('suyaṃ me āusaṃ…', 'I have heard, O long-lived one'); redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous compilation with layers of different ages, fixed in writing at Valabhī in the 5th c. CE.

scholarly.text: Book I old (verse; often placed c. 3rd–2nd c. BCE), Book II later

structure.description: 2 śrutaskandhas: I = 16 lectures (mostly verse), II = 7 lectures (mostly prose)

title: Sthānāṅga Sūtra
summary: The third Aṅga, a numerical compendium arranging doctrinal, cosmological and monastic topics in ten sections from 'ones' to 'tens'; among much else it lists the seven schismatics (nihnavas) and the ten 'wonders' (accheras) of the present era, such as a woman Tīrthaṅkara and the transfer of Mahāvīra's embryo.

attribution.tradition: The meaning (artha) was taught by Mahāvīra; the gaṇadhara Sudharman composed the sūtras and transmitted them to Jambū ('suyaṃ me āusaṃ…', 'I have heard, O long-lived one'); redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous compilation with layers of different ages, fixed in writing at Valabhī in the 5th c. CE.

scholarly.text: compiled over centuries; contains material up to the early centuries CE (e.g. the seven nihnavas)

title: Samavāyāṅga Sūtra
summary: The fourth Aṅga, continuing the numerical arrangement from one to a hundred and then to very large numbers; it describes the contents of all twelve Aṅgas (including the lost Dṛṣṭivāda), the thirty-four supernatural excellences (atiśaya) of a Jina and the thirty-five qualities of his speech, and lists the great persons of the era.

attribution.tradition: The meaning (artha) was taught by Mahāvīra; the gaṇadhara Sudharman composed the sūtras and transmitted them to Jambū ('suyaṃ me āusaṃ…', 'I have heard, O long-lived one'); redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous compilation with layers of different ages, fixed in writing at Valabhī in the 5th c. CE.

scholarly.text: compiled over centuries; its canon description may postdate much of the canon

structure.description: numbered samavāyas from 1 to 100, then larger numbers; appendix on the dvādaśāṅga and the great persons

title: Bhagavatī Sūtra (Vyākhyāprajñapti)
summary: The fifth and largest Aṅga, a vast collection of questions put to Mahāvīra, mostly by Gautama Indrabhūti, on souls, karma, matter, the cosmos, the gods and the path, with narrative sections: the questions of Skandaka and of the laywoman Jayantī, the schism of Jamāli, the followers of Pārśva who accept Mahāvīra, and (śataka 15) the history of Gośāla and his conflict with Mahāvīra. Its answers often distinguish respects (substance, place, time, state), foreshadowing the doctrine of standpoints.

attribution.tradition: The meaning (artha) was taught by Mahāvīra; the gaṇadhara Sudharman composed the sūtras and transmitted them to Jambū ('suyaṃ me āusaṃ…', 'I have heard, O long-lived one'); redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous compilation with layers of different ages, fixed in writing at Valabhī in the 5th c. CE.

tradition.text: the tradition speaks of 36,000 questions answered by Mahāvīra

scholarly.text: a compilation with old and late layers (c. 3rd c. BCE – 5th c. CE)

structure.description: 41 śatakas ('centuries') divided into uddeśakas; opens with the Namaskāra and a salutation to the Brāhmī script

title: Jñātādharmakathā
summary: The sixth Aṅga, teaching by parables and stories: Prince Megha's past life as an elephant, the two tortoises, the four daughters-in-law and the rice grains, the princess Mallī who became the nineteenth Tīrthaṅkara (a woman, in Śvetāmbara belief), Draupadī's story, and others; the second book tells of goddesses who worshipped Mahāvīra.

attribution.tradition: The meaning (artha) was taught by Mahāvīra; the gaṇadhara Sudharman composed the sūtras and transmitted them to Jambū ('suyaṃ me āusaṃ…', 'I have heard, O long-lived one'); redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous compilation with layers of different ages, fixed in writing at Valabhī in the 5th c. CE.

notes: The title's first word is read either as 'examples' (jñāta) or as the Jñāta (Nāya) clan of Mahāvīra.

scholarly.text: c. 1st c. BCE – 5th c. CE (low confidence)

structure.description: 2 śrutaskandhas: I = 19 chapters (jñātas), II = 10 vargas of stories of goddesses

title: Upāsakadaśā
summary: The seventh Aṅga: ten chapters on ten wealthy lay disciples (upāsaka) of Mahāvīra — Ānanda, Kāmadeva, Culanīpitā, Surādeva, Cullaśataka, Kuṇḍakolika, Saddālaputra, Mahāśataka, Nandinīpitā and Sālihīpitā — who take the twelve lay vows, progress through the eleven lay stages (pratimā), withstand divine tests and die peacefully; the Saddālaputra chapter records Mahāvīra's argument against the Ājīvika fatalism.

attribution.tradition: The meaning (artha) was taught by Mahāvīra; the gaṇadhara Sudharman composed the sūtras and transmitted them to Jambū ('suyaṃ me āusaṃ…', 'I have heard, O long-lived one'); redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous compilation with layers of different ages, fixed in writing at Valabhī in the 5th c. CE.

title: Antakṛddaśā
summary: The eighth Aṅga: stories of those who 'made an end' (antakṛt) of rebirth in that very life — among them Gajasukumāla, Kṛṣṇa's young brother, who kept equanimity while a brāhmaṇa set burning coals on his head, and the gardener Arjuna, a murderer who became a monk and bore abuse patiently.

attribution.tradition: The meaning (artha) was taught by Mahāvīra; the gaṇadhara Sudharman composed the sūtras and transmitted them to Jambū ('suyaṃ me āusaṃ…', 'I have heard, O long-lived one'); redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous compilation with layers of different ages, fixed in writing at Valabhī in the 5th c. CE.

title: Anuttaraupapātikadaśā
summary: The ninth Aṅga: stories of monks reborn in the highest (anuttara) heavens, from which they will reach liberation in one more birth — notably Dhanya, whose body wasted by austerities is described limb by limb.

attribution.tradition: The meaning (artha) was taught by Mahāvīra; the gaṇadhara Sudharman composed the sūtras and transmitted them to Jambū ('suyaṃ me āusaṃ…', 'I have heard, O long-lived one'); redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi.

title: Praśnavyākaraṇa
summary: The tenth Aṅga. The extant text treats the five 'doors of inflow' (āsrava: violence, falsehood, theft, unchastity, possessiveness) and the five 'doors of stopping' (saṃvara: the five great vows), with a celebrated list of names and praises of non-harm (ahiṃsā). The Sthānāṅga, Samavāyāṅga and Nandī describe a different original content (questions and answers, including on spells and prognostication); the commentators note the difference.

attribution.tradition: The meaning (artha) was taught by Mahāvīra; the gaṇadhara Sudharman composed the sūtras and transmitted them to Jambū ('suyaṃ me āusaṃ…', 'I have heard, O long-lived one'); redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous compilation with layers of different ages, fixed in writing at Valabhī in the 5th c. CE.

notes: Why the content changed is not recorded with certainty; later tradition says the original was withdrawn because its magical content could be misused (low confidence).

title: Vipākaśruta
summary: The eleventh Aṅga: stories of the ripening (vipāka) of karma — ten of evil deeds bearing painful fruit (such as Mṛgāputra, born a shapeless lump of flesh) and ten of good deeds bearing happy fruit (such as Prince Subāhu).

attribution.tradition: The meaning (artha) was taught by Mahāvīra; the gaṇadhara Sudharman composed the sūtras and transmitted them to Jambū ('suyaṃ me āusaṃ…', 'I have heard, O long-lived one'); redacted at the Valabhī council under Devarddhigaṇi.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous compilation with layers of different ages, fixed in writing at Valabhī in the 5th c. CE.

structure.description: 2 śrutaskandhas: duḥkha-vipāka (10 stories) and sukha-vipāka (10 stories)

Āgama Prakāśana Samiti, Beawar (ed. Madhukar Muni, Sthānakavāsī), Prakrit with Hindi

title: Dṛṣṭivāda
summary: The twelfth Aṅga, lost according to both traditions. As described in the Nandī and Samavāyāṅga it had five parts — parikarma, sūtra, pūrvagata (the fourteen Pūrvas), anuyoga (including the first narrative anuyoga) and cūlikā — and contained all doctrine. The Digambaras hold that portions of two Pūrvas survive in the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa.

attribution.tradition: Composed by the gaṇadharas; the fourteen Pūrvas were known in full last by the śrutakevalin Bhadrabāhu; Sthūlabhadra learned the last four as text only; knowledge of the Pūrvas died out gradually (Śvetāmbara: with Devarddhigaṇi's time; Digambara: within 683 years of the nirvāṇa).

structure.description: 5 parts; the pūrvagata comprised 14 Pūrvas (see cpt:fourteen-purvas)

title: Aupapātika Sūtra
summary: The first Upāṅga (paired with the Ācārāṅga): a model description of the city of Campā, of Mahāvīra's arrival, his assembly and King Kūṇika's visit, his sermon, the kinds of ascetics and the heavens they are reborn in (upapāta), the wanderer Ambaḍa and his disciples, and the state of the liberated (siddha).

attribution.tradition: An aṅgabāhya text composed by the elders (sthavira)

title: Rājapraśnīya
summary: The second Upāṅga: the god Sūryābha's visit to Mahāvīra and his worship of Jina images in his celestial palace, and the dialogue in which Keśin, of Pārśva's line, convinces King Paesi (Pradeśin), who had tried to find the soul by experiments on criminals, that the soul is distinct from the body.
notes: The Paesi dialogue parallels the Pāyāsi Sutta (DN 23) of the Pali canon, where the Buddhist monk Kumāra Kassapa answers King Pāyāsi.

title: Jīvājīvābhigama
summary: The third Upāṅga: an enumeration of living and non-living substances and of the kinds of beings, with a long description of the continents and oceans of the middle world (Jambūdvīpa and beyond).

title: Prajñāpanā Sūtra
summary: The fourth Upāṅga, a systematic treatise in thirty-six sections (pada) on the classification of beings, their locations, lifespans, senses, bodies, sex (veda), passions, leśyās, karma, knowledge and the rest; its first pada lists fifteen kinds of liberated beings, including those liberated in a woman's body, as householders and in the garb of other sects.

attribution.tradition: Composed by Śyāmārya (Ārya Śyāma), a pūrva-knowing elder
attribution.scholarly: c. 1st c. BCE – 1st c. CE (low confidence)

editions.name: Jaina Āgama Series, critical editions, Mahāvīra Jaina Vidyālaya, Bombay (1968–)

title: Sūryaprajñapti
summary: An Upāṅga on astronomy and calendar: the motions of the two suns and two moons of Jambūdvīpa, the lunar mansions and the five-year yuga; nearly identical in content with the Candraprajñapti.
notes: Lists differ on the order of the Sūrya-, Jambūdvīpa- and Candra-prajñaptis (5th–7th Upāṅgas).

title: Jambūdvīpaprajñapti
summary: An Upāṅga describing Jambūdvīpa, the time-cycle of six ages, the life of Ṛṣabha as the founder of civilization and of dharma, and the conquests of the first world-emperor Bharata.

title: Candraprajñapti
summary: An Upāṅga on the moon's course and calendar, nearly identical with the Sūryaprajñapti apart from its opening.

title: Nirayāvalikā (Kalpikā)
summary: The eighth Upāṅga, first of the five 'Nirayāvaliyāo': how King Kūṇika (Ajātaśatru) of Magadha, with his ten half-brothers, fought his grandfather Ceṭaka of Vaiśālī, and how the ten brothers, killed in battle, went to hell.

title: Kalpāvataṃsikā
summary: The ninth Upāṅga: the sons of those princes, who became monks and were reborn in the heavens.

title: Puṣpikā
summary: The tenth Upāṅga: stories of gods (the Moon, the Sun, Śukra, the goddess Bahuputrikā and others) who came to honour Mahāvīra, and of their previous lives.

title: Puṣpacūlikā
summary: The eleventh Upāṅga: stories of goddesses (Śrī, Hrī and others) and their previous lives as nuns.

title: Vṛṣṇidaśā
summary: The twelfth Upāṅga: twelve princes of the Vṛṣṇi (Yādava) clan, such as Niṣadha, who became monks under Ariṣṭanemi.

title: Niśītha Sūtra
summary: The chief Chedasūtra: in twenty sections it lists the transgressions of monks and nuns and the atonement (prāyaścitta) fixed for each. Originally the fifth appendix (cūlā) of the Ācārāṅga ('Ācāraprakalpa'); its bhāṣya and Jinadāsa's cūrṇi are major sources for monastic law and early Jain history.
notes: Chedasūtras were traditionally restricted to mature monks; their study by laypeople was discouraged.

title: Mahāniśītha Sūtra
summary: A Chedasūtra accepted by the Mūrtipūjakas: on confession and atonement, the merit of the Namaskāra mantra, and exemplary stories; it says of itself that it was restored by Haribhadra from a damaged manuscript. Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs reject it.

title: Vyavahāra Sūtra
summary: A Chedasūtra on monastic procedure: confession and atonement, qualifications and duties of office-holders (ācārya, upādhyāya, gaṇin), the five grounds of judgment (āgama, śruta, ājñā, dhāraṇā, jīta), and the course of scriptural study by years of monastic seniority.

title: Bṛhatkalpa Sūtra
summary: A Chedasūtra stating what is allowed (kappa) and not allowed to monks and nuns — lodgings, food, clothes, bowls, travel, contact between the sexes — including the rule that a nun may not be without clothes; with Saṅghadāsa's bhāṣya and Kṣemakīrti's commentary.

title: Daśāśrutaskandha
summary: A Chedasūtra in ten chapters: the twenty faults disturbing concentration (asamādhi-sthāna), the twenty-one grave faults (śabala), the thirty-three disrespects to the teacher (āśātanā), the eight accomplishments of a gaṇin, the ten states of mental concentration, the eleven stages of the layman (upāsaka-pratimā), the twelve special vows of the monk (bhikṣu-pratimā), the Paryuṣaṇākalpa (the Kalpa Sūtra), the thirty sources of deluding karma, and the nine kinds of 'wishing for a reward' (nidāna).

title: Jītakalpa Sūtra
summary: A short Chedasūtra by Jinabhadragaṇi in about a hundred verses, fixing atonements according to 'established practice' (jīta), the last of the five grounds of judgment, for an age without pūrva-knowing teachers.

title: Pañcakalpa
summary: A Chedasūtra on monastic conduct counted in some old lists (instead of the Jītakalpa); the root text is lost, and only a bhāṣya and cūrṇi material are known (low confidence).

title: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra
summary: The first Mūlasūtra, thirty-six chapters of verse and some prose: discipline toward the teacher, the twenty-two hardships, the four rare things, the ignorant and the wise death, the renunciation of Nami, the leaf of the tree ('Gautama, be not careless for a moment'), the outcaste monk Harikeśa, Nemi and Rājīmatī, the dialogue of Keśin and Gautama, the eight 'mothers of the doctrine', the true brāhmaṇa, the path to liberation, austerities, the kinds of karma, the six leśyās and the classes of living and non-living things. Tradition holds that Mahāvīra recited it in his last hours.

attribution.tradition: Mahāvīra's last teaching, given without being asked before his nirvāṇa at Pāvā (Utt 36 end)
attribution.scholarly: an anthology of chapters of different ages, the oldest perhaps c. 3rd–1st c. BCE

tradition.text: spoken by Mahāvīra on the night of his nirvāṇa

scholarly.text: c. 3rd c. BCE – 1st c. CE for most chapters (low confidence)

editions.name: H. Jacobi, Jaina Sūtras Part II (Sacred Books of the East 45), 1895
J. Charpentier, The Uttarādhyayanasūtra, Uppsala 1922

title: Daśavaikālika Sūtra
summary: The second Mūlasūtra, the first text learned by a new Śvetāmbara monk: dharma as non-harm, restraint and austerity; the bee that takes nectar without hurting the flower; the six classes of living beings and the vows; the rules of alms-seeking and speech; conquering the four passions; and the marks of the true monk.

attribution.tradition: Composed by Śayyambhava, the fourth successor of Mahāvīra, from the Pūrvas for his son Manaka, who had only six months to live
attribution.scholarly: early, perhaps c. 3rd–2nd c. BCE (low confidence)

title: Āvaśyaka Sūtra
summary: The Mūlasūtra of the six obligatory daily duties (āvaśyaka): equanimity (sāmāyika), praise of the twenty-four Jinas (caturviṃśatistava, the 'Logassa'), veneration of the teacher (vandana), confession and repentance (pratikramaṇa), abandoning the body in standing meditation (kāyotsarga), and renunciation of specified things for a set time (pratyākhyāna). Its formulas, beginning with the Namaskāra, are the core of Jain liturgy; its niryukti and commentaries carry much narrative.

title: Piṇḍaniryukti
summary: A Mūlasūtra (Mūrtipūjaka list) on the purity of alms (piṇḍa): the faults arising from the donor, from the monk and in the receiving of food, which a mendicant must avoid; with Malayagiri's commentary.

title: Oghaniryukti
summary: A text on the general (ogha) rules of monastic life — inspection, alms, equipment, lodging — counted as the fourth Mūlasūtra in some Mūrtipūjaka lists instead of or together with the Piṇḍaniryukti.

title: Nandī Sūtra
summary: A Cūlikāsūtra (a Mūlasūtra for Sthānakavāsīs): opening hymns to Mahāvīra, the saṅgha and the line of elders, then a treatise on the five kinds of knowledge (mati, śruta, avadhi, manaḥparyaya, kevala), with the classification of scripture (aṅga-praviṣṭa and aṅga-bāhya, kālika and utkālika), the contents of the twelve Aṅgas, and the teaching that the twelve-limbed canon is eternal.

title: Anuyogadvāra Sūtra
summary: A Cūlikāsūtra on the method of exposition, taking 'āvaśyaka' as its example: the four doors (upakrama, nikṣepa, anugama, naya), the fourfold placement of a word's meaning (name, representation, substance, actual state), measures and numbers, the seven notes and the nine sentiments, and the standpoints.

tradition.text: Āryarakṣita (1st c. CE by the traditional chronology)

title: Kalpa Sūtra (Paryuṣaṇākalpa)
summary: Originally the eighth chapter of the Daśāśrutaskandha: (1) the Jinacaritra — the lives of Mahāvīra (in detail: descent, the fourteen dreams, the transfer of the embryo, birth, renunciation, twelve years of austerity, omniscience, rainy seasons, nirvāṇa), Pārśva, Ariṣṭanemi and Ṛṣabha, with the intervals between the other Jinas; (2) the Sthavirāvalī, the line of elders from Mahāvīra's gaṇadharas; (3) the Sāmācārī, rules for monks during the rainy season. Mūrtipūjakas read it aloud during Paryuṣaṇa; richly illustrated manuscripts survive from the 14th c. onward.
genre: biography of the Jinas; monastic rules
alt_titles: Bārasa Sutta (the Prakrit text recited on Saṃvatsarī)

attribution.tradition: Composed by the śrutakevalin Bhadrabāhu (c. 170 years after the nirvāṇa)
attribution.scholarly: the Jinacaritra and Sāmācārī are old; the Sthavirāvalī continues to Devarddhigaṇi (5th c. CE)

tradition.text: Bhadrabāhu, c. 4th c. BCE by the traditional chronology

scholarly.text: core perhaps early centuries BCE; final form 5th c. CE

structure.description: Jinacaritra, Sthavirāvalī, Sāmācārī (c. 1,215 granthas in the usual count)

editions.name: H. Jacobi, Jaina Sūtras Part I (Sacred Books of the East 22), 1884
with Vinayavijaya's Subodhikā commentary (1639), many Gujarati editions

title: Catuḥśaraṇa Prakīrṇaka
summary: A short Prakīrṇaka on taking the four refuges — the Arhats, the Siddhas, the monks and the dharma taught by the omniscient — with confession of wrongs and approval of good deeds.

title: Āturapratyākhyāna
summary: A Prakīrṇaka on the renunciation made by the sick or dying (ātura): the kinds of death (of the ignorant, of the partly wise, of the wise) and the preparation of mind for a peaceful death (restricted theme: summary only).

title: Mahāpratyākhyāna
summary: A Prakīrṇaka of confession, renunciation and reflection for the end of life (restricted theme: summary only).

title: Bhaktaparijñā
summary: A Prakīrṇaka on the renunciation of food at the end of life (bhakta-pratyākhyāna) as the 'death of the wise', with the conditions that must hold and the mental discipline it requires (restricted theme: summary only).

title: Taṇḍulavaicārika
summary: A Prakīrṇaka on the human body: conception and development in the womb, the ten decades of a hundred-year life, the impurity of the body, and the amount of rice (taṇḍula) a person eats in a lifetime — as grounds for detachment.

title: Saṃstāraka
summary: A Prakīrṇaka praising the death-bed of grass (saṃstāraka) of the monk who dies in meditation, with exemplary stories (restricted theme: summary only).

title: Gacchācāra
summary: A Prakīrṇaka on the conduct of the monastic community (gaccha): the good and bad teacher, the discipline of monks and nuns and the relations between them.

title: Gaṇividyā
summary: A Prakīrṇaka on the auspicious days, lunar mansions, hours and omens for monastic acts such as initiation and the beginning of study.

title: Devendrastava
summary: A Prakīrṇaka in which a layman praising the Jina describes to his wife the thirty-two Indras, the classes of gods and their abodes, and the abode of the Siddhas.

title: Maraṇasamādhi
summary: A long Prakīrṇaka on meditative death (maraṇa-samādhi) and the discipline of the dying, with stories of exemplary deaths (restricted theme: summary only).

title: Candravedhyaka
summary: A Prakīrṇaka counted in some lists: on the qualities of teacher and pupil, discipline and concentration at death, with the image of the archer who must pierce the eye of a revolving doll (candravedhya) as a figure for unwavering attention.

title: Vīrastava
summary: A short Prakīrṇaka in some lists praising Mahāvīra through a series of his names and epithets.

title: Ṛṣibhāṣitāni
summary: A collection of sayings of forty-five 'seers' (ṛṣi) called pratyekabuddhas, among them figures known from Brahmanical and Buddhist sources — Nārada, Asita Devala, Aṅgiras, Yājñavalkya, Vajjiyaputta, Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra — as well as Pārśva, Vardhamāna and Maṅkhali Gośāla. The Nandī and the niryukti lists name it, but it is not counted among the forty-five Āgamas.

scholarly.text: often regarded as very old (perhaps c. 3rd–1st c. BCE); low confidence

title: Āvaśyaka Niryukti
summary: The Prakrit verse commentary (niryukti) on the Āvaśyaka, the most important of the ten niryuktis ascribed to Bhadrabāhu: besides explaining terms by the method of nikṣepa it narrates the lives of Ṛṣabha and Mahāvīra, the gaṇadharas' doubts and the schisms (nihnava), and states that the Arhat speaks the meaning and the gaṇadharas compose the sūtras.

attribution.scholarly: a later Bhadrabāhu or anonymous authors, c. 1st–6th c. CE

title: Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya
summary: Jinabhadragaṇi Kṣamāśramaṇa's great verse commentary (c. 3,600 gāthās) on the first (sāmāyika) chapter of the Āvaśyaka: a systematic treatment of the five kinds of knowledge, the standpoints, the debates of Mahāvīra with the eleven gaṇadharas (gaṇadharavāda), and the eight schisms including the Boṭika (Digambara) origin story.

scholarly.text: c. 6th–early 7th c. CE (a manuscript colophon gives Śaka 531 = 609 CE; moderate confidence)

title: Bṛhatkalpa Bhāṣya
summary: Saṅghadāsagaṇi's large verse commentary on the Bṛhatkalpa, an encyclopedia of monastic casuistry and of social life, completed in Sanskrit by Malayagiri and Kṣemakīrti.

title: Niśītha Cūrṇi
summary: Jinadāsagaṇi Mahattara's mixed Prakrit–Sanskrit prose commentary on the Niśītha and its bhāṣya, rich in monastic law, stories (including the Kālaka story) and social history.

title: Āvaśyaka Cūrṇi
summary: Jinadāsa's prose commentary on the Āvaśyaka and its niryukti, one of the richest collections of Jain narratives (lives of the Jinas, Mahāvīra's austerities and hardships, stories of exemplary monks and laymen).

title: Ācārāṅga-ṭīkā of Śīlāṅka
summary: Śīlāṅka's Sanskrit commentary on the Ācārāṅga; with his commentary on the Sūtrakṛtāṅga, the only surviving Sanskrit commentaries on the first two Aṅgas before Abhayadeva.

title: Sūtrakṛtāṅga-ṭīkā of Śīlāṅka
summary: Śīlāṅka's Sanskrit commentary on the Sūtrakṛtāṅga, which identifies and explains the rival doctrines the text refutes.

title: Navāṅgī-vṛtti of Abhayadeva
summary: Abhayadevasūri's Sanskrit commentaries on the third to eleventh Aṅgas (Sthānāṅga to Vipākaśruta), which remain the standard explanations of these texts.

title: Prajñāpanā-vṛtti of Malayagiri
summary: Malayagiri's Sanskrit commentary on the Prajñāpanā, one of many lucid commentaries by this 12th-c. contemporary of Hemacandra on Upāṅgas, the Nandī and Chedasūtras.

title: Āvaśyaka-vṛtti of Haribhadra
summary: Haribhadra's commentary (Śiṣyahitā) on the Āvaśyaka and its niryukti, among the earliest Sanskrit commentaries on the canon; Haribhadra also commented on the Daśavaikālika, Nandī and Anuyogadvāra.

title: Uttarādhyayana-Śiṣyahitā of Śāntisūri
summary: Vādivetāla Śāntisūri's large commentary (Bṛhadvṛtti, also called 'Pāia-ṭīkā') on the Uttarādhyayana.

title: Uttarādhyayana-Sukhabodhā
summary: Devendragaṇi (Nemicandra)'s commentary on the Uttarādhyayana (1073 CE), prized for its Prakrit stories illustrating each chapter.

title: Kalpasūtra-Subodhikā
summary: Vinayavijaya's commentary on the Kalpa Sūtra (1639 CE), the one most used for the public reading of the text during Paryuṣaṇa.

title: Lalitavistarā of Haribhadra
summary: Haribhadra's commentary on the Caityavandana-sūtra (the liturgy of image veneration), explaining the Jina's qualities invoked in the Śakrastava; it quotes the lost 'Yāpanīya-tantra' in support of women's liberation.

title: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra
summary: Hemacandra's Sanskrit epic of the sixty-three 'illustrious persons' of this era — the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras, twelve world-emperors, nine baladevas, nine vāsudevas and nine prativāsudevas — in ten books, ending with a full life of Mahāvīra; written at the request of King Kumārapāla.
alt_titles: Lives of the Sixty-three Illustrious Persons

editions.name: H. M. Johnson, Gaekwad's Oriental Series, 6 vols., 1931–1962

title: Pariśiṣṭaparvan (Sthavirāvalīcarita)
summary: Hemacandra's appendix to the Triṣaṣṭi: the lives of the elders from Jambū, the last omniscient, through Prabhava, Śayyambhava, Bhadrabāhu and Sthūlabhadra to Vajrasvāmin, including the twelve-year famine, the council at Pāṭaliputra and the story of Cāṇakya and Candragupta.

editions.name: ed. H. Jacobi, Bibliotheca Indica, 1883 (2nd ed. 1932)
R. C. C. Fynes, The Lives of the Jain Elders, Oxford World's Classics, 1998

title: Cauppannamahāpurisacariya
summary: Śīlāṅka (Śīlācārya)'s Prakrit prose-and-verse history of the fifty-four 'great men' (the sixty-three less the nine prativāsudevas, who are treated with their vāsudevas).
notes: Whether this Śīlāṅka is the Ācārāṅga commentator is debated.

title: Paumacariya
summary: Vimalasūri's Prakrit Jain Rāmāyaṇa: Rāma (Padma) is a non-violent Jain hero who ends as a liberated monk; Lakṣmaṇa, the vāsudeva, kills Rāvaṇa, a learned vidyādhara rather than a demon; the text rejects the 'false' features of other Rāma stories.

tradition.text: 530 years after Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa, according to its own colophon

title: Vasudevahiṇḍī
summary: Saṅghadāsagaṇi's Prakrit prose romance of the wanderings (hiṇḍī) of Vasudeva, Kṛṣṇa's father, a Jain counterpart of the Bṛhatkathā that frames many stories, including lives of Ṛṣabha and Śānti.

title: Prabhāvakacarita
summary: Prabhācandrasūri's lives of twenty-two influential Śvetāmbara teachers (prabhāvakas), from Vajrasvāmin to Hemacandra (1277 CE).

title: Vividhatīrthakalpa
summary: Jinaprabhasūri's 14th-c. collection of accounts of Jain pilgrimage places (Śatruñjaya, Girnār, Mathurā, Pāvā and many others), their legends and their history.

title: Bhikṣu Granth Ratnākar (collected works of Ācārya Bhikṣu)
summary: The collected Rajasthani verse works of Ācārya Bhikṣu, founder of the Śvetāmbara Terāpanth, setting out his teaching on what is and is not dharma (on compassion, giving, and the nine categories) and the rules of his order (low confidence on the collection's title and contents).
